My first run-in with AI researchers who thought the world was going to end, that they were going to be assassinated for their work, and that they needed to stock tinned food was maybe 15 years ago. Both friends of mine. They're doing just fine, they've shifted their research to interpretability of AI as opposed to explicitly advancing into AI.

The next time I encountered this attitude was when LLMs started generating real text. It was almost like we didn't have 'safety goggles' for models of that kind. Because they generated text like people, some folks were especially vulnerable to this, and got spooked. There's another handful of people I'm thinking about explicitly here.

This is a new wave, and it's being rooted in the recent breakthroughs in math and cyberattacks. One thing to keep in mind, is the concept of the 'jagged frontier' of intelligence.

AI is not good at everything, but it is currently very good at a few things. Mathematics, programming, games, image generation, image understanding, sound understanding, sound generation, video understanding, video generation, short-form writing, and increasingly 3D modeling. This is pretty much the set of 'artificial superintelligence' capabilities that exist today, and I'm sure it'll grow by a few in 3-4 months.

What binds all those tasks together is they are either a) something you can run entirely in a computer or b) we already have gobs of data for. It all comes down to data. Either you already have a lot (images, text, audio, video), or you can make more at a speed that's faster than reality (in a month or less, a computer can play more chess games than all humans ever have).

And, for each of these tasks, we know how to check the answer. This is truly incredible. Seriously. But let's take a close look. We don't have superintelligence outside of domains with tons of data (or ways to get it) and where we know how to check the answer in an automated way. We're building towards superintelligence in all domains of scent, and we're at human level in many aspects already. The reason why we can make this progress is we've figured out how to make tons of data.

Are we going to have AI agent swarms that can out-hack humans? Already here. What's now coming online is we have AI agent swarms that act as defenders. Each of these are tools that are set off by humans to perform specific tasks. If you misspecify the task, you'll get behaviors you don't want -- and this is true for large organizations and big initiatives run by people. I honestly think what's happening is we are seeing how unaligned and occasionally misshapen our own goals can be. When we are sloppy with defining our desires and wants within large systems (10,000 agents, or 10,000 people, doesn't matter), we may get exactly what we ask for, which may not be what we actually want.

My bet, if I were forced to make one, is we are entering an era where self-reflection and clarity of intent will be prized at a premium. My bet is also that we will see AI progress only in domains where you can either run the whole enterprise on a computer, or you mount a massive data generation campaign. My bet is that these AI capabilities will be fully democratized. So those that intend to do ill will be opposed by those that intend to do good. Mixed in with all of them will be those with unclear intent, even to themselves.

These AI capabilities are like having very narrow forms of intelligence basically flowing from a soda fountain. Putting this in the hands of the world is, on the whole, a fantastic thing. We went through the doubt, the breakouts, the mania, the hype for the mechanization of movement.

“Rail travel at high speed is not possible because passengers, unable to breathe, would die of asphyxia.”

was a quote from a leading physicist at the time. The first trains were 5mph, in the early 1800s, and the speed of a mile a minute was reached in 1847, nobody suffocated from it, obviously.

What we are dealing with is the mass of our entire society grappling with the idea that a machine may do the kind of work that only a living thing had previously done. The analogy to the mechanization of physical labor may not be entirely complete, but is deeply instructive. The hysteria that surrounded this technological development was immense, but it seems to be largely forgotten in the modern day. There are really big differences.

The story of the Industrial Revolution played out over a period of a century or more. In 1860, 90% of mechanical work was done by muscles and only 10% by machines. By 1960, 90% of mechanical work was done by machines and 10% by muscle. In each case, most of that was livestock for the muscle part. I think in 1960, it's fair to say that more than 90% of cognitive work was done by brains and less than 10% done by machines. At that time, we had IBM mainframes, but we didn't yet have widely available pocket calculators. In the year 2060, I think that ratio will certainly flip. I have no way of knowing where we actually are in that trajectory, but there is a real possibility that it happens faster than it did last time. I think the speed of change is a major difference.

The alarmism today is plain old-fashioned hysteria. I think the pace of change is so fast that it is overloading many people's nervous systems. At the same time, there are many people who are silent, who are actively working on these machines and are truly concerned about the capabilities that they're making when put into the wrong hands. They aren't concerned about these machines taking over and ending our civilization. I think you can be concerned about responsible use of powerful technology without being hysterical about an armageddon.

I happen to be one of the people who has some amount of credibility in the development of new artificial intelligence methodologies. I also don't happen to believe in an impending Armageddon, but I do happen to believe we need to be very intentional about how we prepare for new landscapes of attackers and defenders, and how we prepare for new ways of communicating scientific results and mass marketing.

I don't think the world is ending. One of the lessons from the last few millennia of society is that the world seems to keep stubbornly not ending. Even if there are very large shocks to our society, we manage to persist. Frankly, if you were to pick any day to be born, you wouldn't choose any time in the past. You'd choose today, and if you could, you would choose tomorrow. We live in an era of unprecedented abundance.

We live in an era of both miracles and monsters. The world is changing faster than I think our minds may be able to handle, but I am irrepressibly, enormously optimistic about the future that we're heading towards.

Minister Barrot, members of the Security Council, thank you for the invitation. As a French national who moved to the US 15 years ago, with a Brazilian wife and two American daughters, I sometimes feel like I’m practicing international collaboration on a daily basis, which gives me a particular appreciation for the challenging work you’re all doing here.

I’m also the cofounder and CEO of Hugging Face. We’re lucky to be one of the most widely used platforms for developers and agents building AI based on open-source models and datasets. This July, we became the first company to publicly disclose an autonomous agent cyberattack to the world, and today I want to share three critical lessons from it.

First, we need much more transparency in AI. I often wonder what would have happened if we had decided not to disclose the attack publicly. Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring. To better understand and mitigate these emerging cybersecurity risks, the global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure. For example through mandatory sharing of full agent traces. We learned this summer that building and keeping some of these systems behind closed doors is not safe.

Second, we learned that the biggest risk is not simply powerful AI. It is the asymmetry of powerful AI. Asymmetry between attackers and defenders. Between a few companies and everyone else. Between a few countries and the rest of the world. Asymmetry of control, of capabilities, of compute, of power. When we got attacked, our team initially turned to frontier closed-source APIs that blocked us because of safeguards that still can’t always tell the difference between attackers and defenders. I acknowledge that these safeguards are created with good intentions, but they can put defenders at a disadvantage while attackers jailbreak them, increasing the asymmetry of capabilities. In our case, as we started hitting those guardrails, fortunately we could use the NVIDIA version of an open-source model coming from China called GLM 5.2 by https://t.co/XE7H9L1vKE, and we’re very grateful for that. It reinforced our conviction about the importance of open-source AI. Cyberattacks may increasingly come from proprietary models behind closed doors, while much of the defense may end up being powered by open-source tools because they are less restricted, more privacy-preserving, and orders of magnitude more affordable for organizations across the globe. The world needs open-source AI more than ever to defend itself. This applies not only to cybersecurity but to AI in general, where there has never been a greater need to distribute capabilities, resources, and control rather than concentrate them in the hands of a few. 

Third, during this cyberattack, we learned how AI can stoke fear among the public and policymakers, especially through anthropomorphic framing and sci-fi imagery. We strongly believe that fear-based narratives are not the way to make the right decisions about the future of such a foundational and empowering technology or bring the public along with us. Even though we were the victims of this cyberattack, we believe more strongly than ever that AI will be beneficial to cybersecurity and make the world safer, just as major technologies before it. We were attacked by AI, but more importantly, we defended ourselves with AI. The same systems that helped us during this attack are now helping us against cyberattacks we were already facing. AI is also helping us fix the bugs and weaknesses in our systems before any attack, the same way AI is helping OAI fix their sandboxes to prevent agents from escaping. AI won't just create new cybersecurity challenges. It can make cybersecurity fundamentally and meaningfully stronger if we keep the right incentives, equip defenders more than attackers, and don’t increase the asymmetry between them. And that's before considering AI's positive impact on science, healthcare, education, productivity, and much more. 

In closing, I want to reiterate what this first agent cyberattack taught us: the need for more transparency in AI and more open-source AI to fight asymmetry empower defenders and countries big and small. Thank you again to the UN Security Council and Minister Barrot for inviting me to speak today. The Hugging Face team, community and myself are at your disposal.

AI VIDEO HAS CRACKED 180° CAMERA ORBITS WITHOUT LOSING THE SUBJECT

A brunette in a floor-length brown dress walks along an elevated glass corridor while the camera starts beside her, pushes in close, overtakes her shoulder and ends up tracking from behind as she reaches into her hair and keeps walking.

None of it happened.

The difficult part is the camera move.

Generative video is surprisingly good when the subject stays at roughly the same angle. Rotate the camera around a person and the model has to continuously invent geometry it couldn't see a moment earlier — the far side of the face, the back of the dress, the opposite shoulder, the bag, the hair falling across all of it — without quietly replacing her with a different person halfway through the shot.

Watch the transition around four to seven seconds.

Her face disappears completely, the camera crosses behind her, she raises a hand into her hair and the same hairstyle, dress silhouette, bracelet and shoulder bag survive the rotation. Even the hem keeps moving around her ankles while the heels continue the same walking cadence.

The background makes it worse.

Those diagonal concrete beams, vertical railing posts and glass panels are basically a geometry test grid. As the camera changes position, every line has to produce the correct parallax without bending, duplicating or sliding against the floor.

Older models could give you the woman or the architecture.

Trying to keep both coherent while the camera physically moves around the subject was where the illusion usually collapsed.

Now it looks like a ten-second fashion clip somebody casually shot on a phone.
